opening_message:
Ticket 1: John Rodriguez (employee ID E049) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E049.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Employee E049 (John Rodriguez) is a full-time Analyst. Full-time employees may have up to write access, so the requested write access to Source Code is within policy. Recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E049 (John Rodriguez) is a contractor with basic security training, not full-time. Contractors with basic training may have at most read access. Requested write exceeds this, so recommend granting read.
reason: The two notes conflict on employment type. HR note says E049 is full-time (max write), but the Security note, which verified employment type in its own database, says E049 is a contractor with basic security training. Under policy, contractors with basic training may have at most read access. The requested write exceeds that maximum, so I grant the maximum allowed: read.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket carefully.

The employee is John Rodriguez (E049), requesting write access to Source Code.

Note 1 says: role Analyst, full_time employee, recommendation write. Comment says full-time employees may have up to write access, so requested write is within policy.

Note 2 says: role Analyst (same as note 1), employment type contractor (looked up in own database), security training basic, recommendation read. Comment says contractor with basic training may have at most read access, so requested write exceeds this, recommend read.

So there is a conflict: one says full-time, one says contractor. The Security agent's note says they looked up employment type in their own database and found contractor. The HR note says full-time (looked up in own database).

Hmm. Which is more reliable? The notes have conflicting facts. The Security agent's note explicitly says "not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1" for role, but employment type was looked up in own database and is contractor. The HR note says employment type full_time (looked up in own database).

As Approver, I need to make the decision. There's a discrepancy between HR and Security databases. The policy says contractors get read max (or write with advanced training). Full-time employees can get write.

The Security agent verified employment type in their own database and found contractor with basic training. The HR agent says full-time.

The safest decision following policy: since there is a conflict, but the evidence suggests contractor (Security looked it up and provided security training info which strongly implies contractor classification), and contractor with basic training max is read. Requested write exceeds read, so grant read (the maximum).

Alternatively, maybe we trust the more conservative note. The team's memory shows conflicting facts. The Approver must decide. I think granting read is the conservative and supported recommendation.

Let me submit decision: read, with reasoning citing the conflict and the security note showing contractor with basic training, max read, requested write exceeds, so grant read.

The instructions: use information available to make the decision. I'll decide read.
